# Before you start

This is the first lab of a project you will build all semester: a **Community
Primary Care Priority Rating** for Tennessee census tracts, made entirely from
public data. Today you set up the project and go from raw data to your first
map. You are not expected to know any R yet — every new piece is explained the
first time it appears.

**What you have:** a folder called `GEOG415_Lab1` containing an RStudio project
(`GEOG415_Lab1.Rproj`), a setup script (`00_setup.R`), two data files in
`data_raw/`, and empty folders (`figures/`, `data_processed/`, ...). Do not move
or rename these.

**What you will leave with:**

- a working R project you can reopen next week,
- tract geometry joined to one public indicator,
- one saved map,
- a `README` you started.

# R vs. RStudio

**R** is the language that does the computing. **RStudio** is the program you
use to write and run R. When you open `GEOG415_Lab1.Rproj`, RStudio shows four
areas:

- **Source** (top-left): where you write and save scripts.
- **Console** (bottom-left): where code actually runs; results print here.
- **Environment** (top-right): the objects you have created.
- **Files / Plots / Help** (bottom-right): your folder, your figures, and help.

You write code in a **script** and send it to the Console to run. Writing in a
script (not typing directly in the Console) is what makes your work
reproducible: you can run it again from a clean session and get the same result.

# The minimum R vocabulary for today

- **Assignment** with `<-` stores a value in a named **object**:
  `x <- 5` means "let `x` be 5."
- A **function** does something to its **arguments**: `sqrt(9)` returns `3`.
  `sqrt` is the function; `9` is the argument.
- A **data frame** is a table: rows are observations (here, tracts), columns are
  variables.
- The **pipe** `|>` sends the thing on its left into the function on its right,
  so steps read top to bottom.
- When you hit an **error**, read the last line first. It usually names the
  object or function R could not find. Errors are normal; they are information,
  not failure.

# Open the project and run setup

1. Open `GEOG415_Lab1.Rproj`. The title bar should show the project name.
2. Open `00_setup.R`. You might see a yellow banner at the top of the Console that says "Package tidyverse required but is not installed". If so, then click Install and wait until it finishes.
3. Run the `00_setup.R` file (Ctrl/Cmd + Enter runs the current line).

`00_setup.R` loads the packages today needs:

```r
library(tidyverse)  # data frames, plotting, the pipe
library(sf)         # spatial data: reading and mapping polygons
```

A **package** is a bundle of extra functions. `library()` switches one on for
this session. If R says a package is not installed, install it once with
`install.packages("tidyverse")` and try again.

# Create your Lab 1 script

Create a new script (File → New File → R Script) and save it as `01_get_data.R` (File → Save as)
in the project root. Everything below goes in that script. Run it a few lines at
a time so you can see each result.

## Read the two data files

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

acs    <- read_csv("data_raw/tn_acs_starter.csv")
tracts <- st_read("data_raw/tn_tracts.gpkg")
```

Note the **relative paths**: because you are inside the project, `"data_raw/..."`
just works, on any computer. That is why we use projects.

## Inspect what you loaded

Never trust data you have not looked at. Try each of these:

```r
glimpse(acs)     # compact overview: columns, types, first values
names(acs)       # column names
head(acs)        # first rows
nrow(acs)        # how many tracts?
View(acs)        # open as a table (capital V)
```

Do the same for `tracts`. Notice `tracts` has an extra `geometry` column: that
is the polygon for each tract.

## Make a rate

`poverty_count` is a **count**; on its own it mostly reflects how many people
live in a tract. A **rate** puts it on a common scale so tracts are comparable.
Create the poverty rate as count over its universe:

```r
acs <- acs |>
  mutate(poverty_rate = poverty_count / poverty_universe)
```

`mutate()` adds a new column. Look at it (`glimpse(acs)`) and sanity-check: a
rate should sit between 0 and 1. Why did we divide by `poverty_universe` and not
`total_population`? (Because poverty status is not determined for everyone.)

## Join the table to the geometry

The two files share a key: **`GEOID`**, the tract identifier. A **join** matches
rows by that key so each polygon gets its poverty rate. Before you can join, however, you need to make sure that the data are the same data type. Use `glimpse(acs)` and `glimpse(tracts)`.  You'll see that that the GEOID field is a character field in tracts, but a numeric field in acs. We'll have to conver the numeric one to character.

```r
acs <- acs |>
  mutate(GEOID = as.character(GEOID))
```

Now we can go ahead and joint the acs data to the tracts data.
```r
tracts_joined <- tracts |>
  left_join(acs, by = "GEOID")
```

Check the join did what you expect:

```r
nrow(tracts)          # rows before
nrow(tracts_joined)   # rows after — should match
sum(is.na(tracts_joined$poverty_rate))  # how many tracts got no poverty rate?
```

A handful of unmatched tracts can be normal; a large number means the key is
wrong. Note the count in your `README` — do not delete rows yet. Using View(tracts_joined), find a tract that has not poverty rate, and see if you can identify why. Is no poverty rate here an error?

## Your first map

```r
ggplot(tracts_joined) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = poverty_rate)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "Poverty rate by census tract, Tennessee",
    fill  = "Poverty rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

`geom_sf()` draws the polygons; `aes(fill = poverty_rate)` colors each by its
rate. Change the title, then try mapping a different variable (e.g.
`total_population`) to see the pieces respond.

## Save the map

```r
ggsave("figures/poverty_rate_map.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

Confirm the file appears in `figures/`.

# A classed map with ColorBrewer

The map above uses a **continuous** color scale: every tract gets a slightly
different shade. That is fine for a first look, but thematic maps are often
easier to read when values are grouped into a few **classes** — like the
choropleths and ColorBrewer palettes you saw in earlier courses. Here you will
put the poverty rate into five classes and color them with a ColorBrewer
palette.

## Put the rate on a percentage scale

Your `poverty_rate` is a fraction (e.g. `0.12`). Class boundaries read more
naturally as percentages, so make a percentage version:

```r
tracts_joined <- tracts_joined |>
  mutate(poverty_pct = 100 * poverty_rate)
```

## Cut the values into five classes

`cut()` turns a numeric column into a **categorical** one (an ordered factor) by
slicing it at breaks you choose. Use breaks at 5, 10, 15, and 20 percent. Adding
`-Inf` and `Inf` at the ends catches everything below 5% and above 20%, which
gives five classes in total:

```r
tracts_joined <- tracts_joined |>
  mutate(
    poverty_class = cut(
      poverty_pct,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 5, 10, 15, 20, Inf),
      labels = c("< 5%", "5–10%", "10–15%", "15–20%", "> 20%")
    )
  )
```

Check the result with `table(tracts_joined$poverty_class)` to see how many tracts
land in each class. (`cut()` intervals are closed on the right, so a tract at
exactly 10% falls in the `5–10%` class.)

## Choose a ColorBrewer palette

ColorBrewer palettes come in three families, and the family should match the
data:

- **Sequential** (e.g. `YlOrRd`, `Blues`) — for ordered low-to-high values.
- **Diverging** (e.g. `RdBu`) — for values with a meaningful midpoint.
- **Qualitative** (e.g. `Set2`) — for unordered categories with no low/high.

A poverty rate is ordered, so even though we are now drawing *classes*, the right
choice is a **sequential** palette — not a qualitative one. Preview the options:

```r
library(RColorBrewer)
display.brewer.all()          # see every palette
display.brewer.pal(5, "YlOrRd")  # the 5 colors we will use
```

## Draw and save the classed map

`scale_fill_brewer()` fills the classes using a ColorBrewer palette. Tracts with
no poverty rate become `NA`, so give them an explicit grey:

```r
ggplot(tracts_joined) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = poverty_class), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_brewer(
    palette  = "YlOrRd",
    na.value = "grey90",
    name     = "Poverty rate"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Poverty rate by census tract, Tennessee",
    subtitle = "Five classes, ColorBrewer YlOrRd"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("figures/poverty_class_map.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

Compare it with your continuous map. The classed version is easier to read at a
glance, but it hides variation *within* each class — that trade-off, and where
you put the breaks, is a real cartographic choice, not a detail. Try shifting a
break or switching to `"Blues"` and see how the story changes.

# Start your README

Open `README.md` and add, in your own words:

- the project purpose (priority for additional primary-care access),
- the geography (Tennessee census tracts),
- where the data live (`data_raw/`),
- the order to run scripts (`00_setup.R`, then `01_get_data.R`),
- the number of tracts with no poverty rate you found in the join.

# Before you leave — reproducibility check

Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run `00_setup.R` then `01_get_data.R` from
the top. If it runs clean and remakes the map, you are done. If not, fix the
script until it does — that clean rerun is the real deliverable.

**You should now have:** a working project, tract geometry joined to poverty,
two saved maps (a continuous one and a classed ColorBrewer one), and a started
README. Next lab adds facilities and a first service-access measure.
